> **What this document is.** The first Study B question: do pill, injectable
> and vaginal ring users have differently *composed* vaginal microbiomes?
> This is the microbiome half of the week — the same kind of analysis as
> Tuesday's ordination module, but now testing the three arms against each
> other. We start with a map (ordination), then a formal test of the map
> (PERMANOVA), then ask whether any individual species differ
> (DESeq2 on raw counts). Full data QC lives in `01-qc.html`; this document
> repeats only the checks this analysis depends on.

```{r setup}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(DESeq2)
library(microViz)
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(patchwork)   # lets p_arm + p_com put two plots side by side

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

d  <- read_counts("group_b")
sp <- d$species         # 220 species x 93 samples, RAW counts
md <- d$metadata        # one row per sample, same order as the columns

# Community type, same rule as 01-qc and notebook 02: Lactobacillus genus
# >= half of the sample's species reads. Used only to label the right-hand
# ordination panel — the tests below use arm, from the metadata.
lacto_taxa <- d$taxonomy |> filter(Genus == "Lactobacillus") |> pull(taxon)
lacto_frac <- colSums(sp[lacto_taxa, , drop = FALSE]) / colSums(sp)
md$community <- ifelse(lacto_frac >= 0.5, "lactobacillus", "anaerobe")
```

# 1. QC for this analysis

```{r qc-checks}
#| label: qc-checks
stopifnot(identical(colnames(sp), md$sample_id))  # order check: a silent
                                                  # mismatch would ruin everything
knitr::kable(table(Arm = md$arm, `RNA-seq batch` = md$rnaseq_batch),
             caption = "Samples per arm and sequencing batch")
```

- **Order check passed:** species-table columns and metadata rows are in the
  same `sample_id` order.
- **Sample sizes:** 28 pill, 39 injectable, 26 ring (93 total). The ring arm
  is the smallest, so ring comparisons carry the least power.
- **Carried flags from `01-qc.html`:** nine samples sit below half the median
  microbiome library size (lowest `B006` at 5,247 reads); `B030` is 99.8 %
  *Lactobacillus iners* (real biology, but it can pull ordinations); `B018`
  and `B029` lack cytokines (irrelevant here). None is dropped — the
  ordination in section 2 is the check that no flagged sample sits wildly
  alone.

# 2. Ordination: do the three arms separate?

We transform to CLR (centred log-ratio — each species compared against the
geometric mean of the sample, the standard way to handle compositional data)
and draw a Euclidean PCoA. Points are coloured by arm; the right panel
reminds us what the *big* structure in this table actually is: community
type, not method.

```{r ordination}
#| label: ordination
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Species-table PCoA (CLR + Euclidean). Left: coloured by method. Right: coloured by community type — the structure that actually separates."
ps <- as_counts(dataset = "group_b", table = "microbiome", data = d)
sd <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame")
idx <- match(sd$sample_id, md$sample_id)
sd$arm       <- md$arm[idx]
sd$community <- md$community[idx]
sample_data(ps) <- sample_data(sd)

ord <- ps |>
  tax_transform("clr", zero_replace = "halfmin") |>
  dist_calc("euclidean") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA")

eig <- attr(ord, "ord")$CA$eig
sh  <- round(100 * eig / sum(eig), 1)

p_arm <- ord_plot(ord, axes = 1:2, color = "arm") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = arm), type = "norm", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "By method", x = sprintf("Axis 1 (%s%%)", sh[1]),
       y = sprintf("Axis 2 (%s%%)", sh[2]), colour = "Arm")
p_com <- ord_plot(ord, axes = 1:2, color = "community") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = community), type = "norm", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "By community type", x = sprintf("Axis 1 (%s%%)", sh[1]),
       y = NULL, colour = "Community")
p_arm + p_com
```

No sample sits in obvious isolation, so none of the flagged low-depth
samples needs dropping.

# 3. PERMANOVA: a formal test of the map

PERMANOVA asks whether samples from different arms are further apart, on
average, than samples from the same arm, and gets a p-value by shuffling the
arm labels 9,999 times. R² is the share of all the between-sample variation
the arm explains. Batch is included in the same model with `by = "margin"`
so each term gets its own adjusted test
([Anderson 2001](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1442-9993.2001.01070.pp.x)).

```{r permanova}
#| label: permanova
dm <- attr(ord, "dist")
meta_p <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))[rownames(as.matrix(dm)), ]
meta_p$arm <- factor(meta_p$arm, levels = c("ring", "pill", "injectable"))
set.seed(1)
main <- adonis2(dm ~ arm + rnaseq_batch, data = meta_p,
                permutations = 9999, by = "margin")
disp <- permutest(betadisper(dm, meta_p$arm), permutations = 9999)

pair <- function(a, b) {
  keep <- meta_p$arm %in% c(a, b)
  out  <- adonis2(as.dist(as.matrix(dm)[keep, keep]) ~ arm,
                  data = droplevels(meta_p[keep, ]), permutations = 9999)
  tibble(comparison = paste(a, "vs", b),
         n = sum(keep),
         `share of variation (%)` = round(100 * out$R2[1], 1),
         `p (raw)` = out$`Pr(>F)`[1])
}
pairs <- bind_rows(pair("ring", "pill"),
                   pair("ring", "injectable"),
                   pair("pill", "injectable")) |>
  mutate(`p (adjusted, BH)` = p.adjust(`p (raw)`, "BH"))

q1_r2  <- round(100 * main$R2[1], 1)   # row 1 = arm (margin test)
q1_p   <- round(main$`Pr(>F)`[1], 3)
q1_rp  <- round(pairs$`p (raw)`[2], 3)
q1_ra  <- round(pairs$`p (adjusted, BH)`[2], 3)
q1_sp2 <- pairs$`share of variation (%)`[2]
q1_dp  <- round(disp$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1], 2)
```

```{r permanova-table}
#| label: permanova-table
knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    test = c("arm (adjusted for batch)", "batch (adjusted for arm)",
             "spread check (betadisper)"),
    n = c(93, 93, 93),
    `share of variation (%)` = round(100 * c(main$R2[1], main$R2[2], NA), 1),
    p = round(c(main$`Pr(>F)`[1], main$`Pr(>F)`[2],
                disp$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1]), 3)
  ),
  caption = "PERMANOVA on species (CLR + Euclidean, 9,999 permutations)"
)
knitr::kable(pairs |>
               mutate(`p (raw)` = round(`p (raw)`, 3),
                      `p (adjusted, BH)` = round(`p (adjusted, BH)`, 3)),
             caption = "Each pair of arms separately (9,999 permutations)")
```

- **Main test:** the three arms explain `r q1_r2` % of
  the species-level variation, p = `r q1_p`
  (n = 93). **Not significant.**
- **Pairwise:** no pair survives adjustment; the largest raw effect is ring
  vs injectable at `r q1_sp2` %
  (raw p = `r q1_rp`, adjusted
  `r q1_ra`).
- **Spread check:** the arms do not differ in how *scattered* they are
  (p = `r q1_dp`), so PERMANOVA is not being fooled
  by a difference in spread.

> **Sanity check.** Change `set.seed(1)` to another number and re-render —
> the R² must stay exactly `r q1_r2` % and the p-value
> should stay near `r q1_p`. You can also verify the
> R² by hand: it is the between-arm sum of squares divided by the total,
> both printed by `adonis2`.

# 4. Differential abundance: do any individual species differ?

The ordination tests the whole profile at once; small shifts in a few
species could still hide inside a non-significant map. DESeq2 tests each
species separately. It takes **raw counts** (it does its own
normalisation — never CPM or logged values) and, like the ordination, gets
batch as a covariate. We first ask "does *any* arm differ?" with a
likelihood-ratio test, then look at each pair.

```{r deseq}
#| label: deseq
sp_f <- sp[rowSums(sp >= 10) >= 10, ]    # same filter rule as the gene analyses
dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(sp_f, md, design = ~ rnaseq_batch + arm),
             quiet = TRUE)
lrt <- as.data.frame(results(DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(sp_f, md, ~ rnaseq_batch + arm),
                                   test = "LRT", reduced = ~ rnaseq_batch,
                                   quiet = TRUE))) |>
  rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
  left_join(d$taxonomy |> select(taxon, Genus, species), by = "taxon") |>
  mutate(padj = replace_na(padj, 1))

pair_res <- function(a, b) {
  as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("arm", a, b))) |>
    rownames_to_column("taxon") |>
    left_join(d$taxonomy |> select(taxon, Genus, species), by = "taxon") |>
    mutate(padj = replace_na(padj, 1))
}
ring_pill <- pair_res("ring", "pill")
ring_inj  <- pair_res("ring", "injectable")
pill_inj  <- pair_res("pill", "injectable")
```

```{r deseq-table}
#| label: deseq-table
expected <- function(r) round(0.05 * sum(!is.na(r$pvalue)))
knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    comparison = c("any arm differs (LRT)", "ring vs pill", "ring vs injectable",
                   "pill vs injectable"),
    samples = c("93", "26 vs 28", "26 vs 39", "28 vs 39"),
    `species at FDR < 0.05` = c(sum(lrt$padj < 0.05),
                                sum(ring_pill$padj < 0.05),
                                sum(ring_inj$padj < 0.05),
                                sum(pill_inj$padj < 0.05)),
    `raw p < 0.05` = c(sum(lrt$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       sum(ring_pill$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       sum(ring_inj$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       sum(pill_inj$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `expected by chance` = c(expected(lrt), expected(ring_pill),
                             expected(ring_inj), expected(pill_inj))
  ),
  caption = "DESeq2 on species (raw counts, batch-adjusted)"
)
```

```{r deseq-top}
#| label: deseq-top
top <- lrt |> filter(padj < 0.05) |>
  slice_min(padj, n = 10) |>
  transmute(species = str_c(Genus, " ", species),
            FDR = signif(padj, 2))
knitr::kable(top, caption = "Smallest-FDR species in the any-arm test")
```

- The hit counts sit **at or below what chance alone would give**
  (220 species tested → about 11 expected at raw p < 0.05). Whatever small
  shifts exist are not concentrated in particular species.
- One caveat that always applies here: these tables are
  **compositional** — "higher relative abundance" is not the same claim as
  "there was more of it".

> **Sanity check.** Pick the top species in the table, take its raw counts
> from `02_microbiome_counts.csv`, and compare the ring-arm median with the
> pill-arm median by eye — a striking visual gap should match a small FDR,
> and here you should see mostly overlapping clouds, consistent with the
> non-significant tests.

# 5. Verdict

- **The three methods do not differ detectably in community composition.**
  Ordination: no visible separation (n = 93). PERMANOVA: 2.8 %, p = 0.17;
  no pairwise comparison survives adjustment. DESeq2: hit counts at
  chance level, no species stands out.
- The strong structure in this table is **community type**
  (48 lactobacillus-dominant vs 45 anaerobe samples, axis 1 = 36 %) — and
  community type is *balanced across the arms*, which is why the method
  comparison is not chasing it. Question 3
  (`06-q3-community-vs-method.html`) follows that split into the genes.
- With 26–39 people per arm, a real but modest effect could still hide
  here; absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

## Choices made

- **CLR + Euclidean** for the ordination and PERMANOVA, because species
  profiles are compositional; Bray-Curtis on raw counts and Jaccard on
  presence/absence were the alternatives and give the same picture (see
  `01-qc.html`, section 9).
- **Species table left unfiltered** for the ordination, matching
  `01-qc.html`; the DESeq2 abundance test filters at ≥ 10 reads in ≥ 10
  samples, the same rule as the gene analyses — a laxer rule spends tests on
  near-empty species, a stricter one loses power.
- **PERMANOVA with batch in one model, `by = "margin"`, 9,999 permutations**
  — the correction from `03-three-arms-review.html`; the default sequential
  test gives the first term credit for anything it shares with the second.
  The batch label is the RNA-seq run, the only batch information the
  metadata carries; if the microbiome was sequenced in different runs, that
  variable is not available to adjust for.
- **Likelihood-ratio test** for "does any arm differ?" (2 df) before any
  pairwise look; jumping straight to pairwise tests is the alternative and
  invites cherry-picking.
- **BH adjustment** for the pairwise PERMANOVA p-values; Bonferroni is the
  stricter alternative.
- **Kept all 93 samples**, including the nine low-depth ones and the `B030`
  near-monoculture; dropping them is the alternative but none drives the
  (null) result, and CLR with half-min replacement handles the zeros.
- **Did not adjust for vaginal pH** here — pH differs by arm (p = 0.02) and
  could be on the causal path from hormones to microbiome; an adjusted model
  is the alternative and belongs in a follow-up rather than a null-result
  document.
